entries.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Sine Wave
entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the complex Fourier series coefficients of a sine wave by converting it into positive and negative fundamental-frequency complex exponentials and identifying the nonzero harmonic coefficients that determine its magnitude and phase spectra.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Sine Wave
sections.section_title: Converting a Sine Wave into Complex Exponentials

prompt_blocks.text: Which exponential rewrite is equivalent to $x(t)=-\sin(\omega_0 t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Negating the sine flips the order of the two fundamental-frequency exponentials but keeps the same two harmonic slots. The cosine form, the one-term form, and the doubled-frequency form all change the move in the wrong way.

prompt_blocks.text: Which exponential rewrite is equivalent to $x(t)=2\sin(\omega_0 t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Amplitude multiplies both exponential terms equally, so the unit-sine rewrite is scaled by 2 and the same $k=\pm1$ structure stays in place. The other choices either miss the amplitude, change the sign pattern, or switch to the wrong harmonic frequency.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Sine Wave
sections.section_title: Identifying the k = 1 and k = -1 Coefficients

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)=\frac{3}{2j}e^{j\omega_0 t}-\frac{3}{2j}e^{-j\omega_0 t}$, which choice gives the nonzero Fourier coefficients?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The $e^{j\omega_0 t}$ term is the $k=1$ harmonic and the $e^{-j\omega_0 t}$ term is the $k=-1$ harmonic. Multiply the example coefficients by $3$, and every other $c_k$ stays zero because no other harmonics appear.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)=-\frac{1}{2j}e^{j\omega_0 t}+\frac{1}{2j}e^{-j\omega_0 t}$, what are $c_1$ and $c_{-1}$ in rectangular form?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: This is the same $k=\pm 1$ pattern with the sign flipped. Since $\frac{1}{2j}=-\frac{j}{2}$, the coefficient in front of $e^{j\omega_0 t}$ becomes $\frac{j}{2}$ and the coefficient in front of $e^{-j\omega_0 t}$ becomes $-\frac{j}{2}$.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Sine Wave
sections.section_title: Including Amplitude in Sine-Wave Coefficients

prompt_blocks.text: Which coefficient pair matches the complex Fourier coefficients of $x(t)=3\sin(\omega_0 t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The amplitude multiplies both nonzero coefficients. Start from the unit-sine pair and scale by 3.
No other harmonic changes, so the coefficient pattern is still sparse at $k=\pm1$.

prompt_blocks.text: Which coefficient pair matches the complex Fourier coefficients of $x(t)=-\frac{1}{2}\sin(\omega_0 t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the same two harmonic slots and scale them by $A=-\frac{1}{2}$. The sign flip and the halving both matter.
The amplitude changes only the size and sign of the existing pair; it does not create any new coefficients.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Sine Wave
sections.section_title: Including Sinusoidal Phase in the Coefficients

prompt_blocks.text: Which pair of complex Fourier coefficients is correct for $x(t)=3\sin(\omega_0 t+\pi/6)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Carry the phase through the same two exponential slots: the $k=1$ coefficient gets $e^{j\phi}$ and the $k=-1$ coefficient gets $e^{-j\phi}$. The amplitude $A=3$ scales both coefficients, and no other harmonics appear.

prompt_blocks.text: Which pair of complex Fourier coefficients is correct for $x(t)=5\sin(\omega_0 t-\pi/4)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The same coefficient pattern still applies: the positive-frequency term gets the phase factor $e^{j\phi}$ and the negative-frequency term gets $e^{-j\phi}$. Here $\phi=-\pi/4$, so the phase factors reverse direction, and the amplitude $A=5$ scales both coefficients.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Sine Wave
sections.section_title: Reading Magnitude and Phase from Sine-Wave Coefficients

prompt_blocks.text: A signal has coefficients $c_1=-j$ and $c_{-1}=j$, with $c_k=0$ for $k\neq \pm1$. Which magnitude/phase spectrum description is correct?

choice_blocks.text: Equal nonzero lines at $k=\pm1$: $|c_1|=|c_{-1}|=1$, $\arg(c_1)=-\pi/2$, $\arg(c_{-1})=\pi/2$, and all other coefficients are zero.
The nonzero spectrum entries are $c_1=-j$ and $c_{-1}=j$, so the magnitude spectrum is $-j$ at $k=1$ and $j$ at $k=-1$.
One nonzero line at $k=1$ with $|c_1|=1$ and $\arg(c_1)=-\pi/2$; every other coefficient is zero.
Equal nonzero lines at $k=\pm1$: $|c_1|=|c_{-1}|=1$, but the phases are $\arg(c_1)=\pi/2$ and $\arg(c_{-1})=-\pi/2$.
Equal lines at $k=\pm1$ with $|c_1|=|c_{-1}|=1$ and a DC line $|c_0|=1$.

questions.correct_answer: Equal lines at $k=\pm1$ with magnitude 1 and phases $-\pi/2$ and $\pi/2$; all other coefficients are zero.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Take the modulus of each complex coefficient to get the magnitude spectrum. Since $|-j|=|j|=1$, the two nonzero lines both have magnitude 1, and their phases are the arguments of the coefficients: $-\pi/2$ for $-j$ and $\pi/2$ for $j$. All other harmonic slots stay zero.

prompt_blocks.text: A signal has coefficients $c_1=2e^{-j\pi/4}$ and $c_{-1}=2e^{j\pi/4}$, with $c_k=0$ for $k\neq \pm1$. Which magnitude/phase spectrum description is correct?

choice_blocks.text: Equal nonzero lines at $k=\pm1$: $|c_1|=|c_{-1}|=2$, $\arg(c_1)=-\pi/4$, $\arg(c_{-1})=\pi/4$, and all other coefficients are zero.
Equal nonzero lines at $k=\pm1$: $|c_1|=|c_{-1}|=4$, $\arg(c_1)=-\pi/4$, $\arg(c_{-1})=\pi/4$, and all other coefficients are zero.
One nonzero line at $k=1$ with $|c_1|=2$ and $\arg(c_1)=-\pi/4$; every other coefficient is zero.
Equal nonzero lines at $k=\pm1$: $|c_1|=|c_{-1}|=2$, but the phases are $\arg(c_1)=\pi/4$ and $\arg(c_{-1})=-\pi/4$.
Equal nonzero lines at $k=\pm1$: $|c_1|=|c_{-1}|=2$, and the spectrum is just the coefficient pair $2e^{-j\pi/4}$ and $2e^{j\pi/4}$.

questions.correct_answer: Equal lines at $k=\pm1$ with magnitude 2 and phases $-\pi/4$ and $\pi/4$; all other coefficients are zero.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read each coefficient in polar form: the magnitude is the absolute value of the complex number, and the phase is its angle. Both coefficients have magnitude 2, while the angles are $-\pi/4$ and $\pi/4$. Since every other coefficient is zero, the spectrum has only the two $k=\pm1$ lines.

entries.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Rectangular Periodic Signal
entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the complex Fourier series coefficients of a rectangular periodic signal by recognizing that only the pulse-support interval contributes to the one-period coefficient integral and evaluating the resulting exponential integral in terms of amplitude, width, period, and harmonic index.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Rectangular Periodic Signal
sections.section_title: Reading Amplitude, Pulse Width, and Period from a Rectangular Signal

image_slots.image_description: A clean rectangular periodic signal plot with one pulse per period. Show a single pulse starting at t=0, with height labeled 4, horizontal width labeled 3, and the next identical pulse beginning 10 time units later so the period is clearly 10. Label the time axis. Highlight the pulse-support interval 0 <= t < 3. Keep the plot uncluttered, educational, and visually centered on the parameter-reading task.

A clean rectangular periodic signal plot with one pulse per period. Show a single pulse starting at t=0, with height labeled 6, horizontal width labeled 4, and the next identical pulse beginning 12 time units later so the period is clearly 12. Keep the plot uncluttered, educational, and visually centered on the parameter-reading task.

prompt_blocks.text: From the plot, what are $A$, $\tau$, and $T$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The pulse height gives $A=4$, the on-interval from $t=0$ to $t=3$ gives $\tau=3$, and the spacing to the next identical pulse gives $T=10$. So the parameter triple is $(A,\tau,T)=(4,3,10)$.

prompt_blocks.text: From the plot, what are $A$, $\tau$, and $T$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The pulse height gives $A=6$, the on-interval gives $\tau=4$, and the repeat spacing gives $T=12$. So the correct parameter triple is $(A,\tau,T)=(6,4,12)$.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Rectangular Periodic Signal
sections.section_title: Restricting the Coefficient Integral to the Pulse Support

prompt_blocks.text: Given $x(t)=2A$ on $0\le t<\tau$ and $0$ on $\tau\le t<T$, which expression is the coefficient integral after restricting to the pulse support?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Only the pulse-support interval contributes because $x(t)=0$ on $\tau\le t<T$. Factor out the constant amplitude $2A$, keep the $1/T$ factor, and restrict the integral to $0\le t<\tau$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $x(t)=A$ on $0\le t<2\tau$ and $0$ on $2\tau\le t<T$, which expression is the coefficient integral after restricting to the pulse support?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The nonzero part of the signal runs over $0\le t<2\tau$, so that is the only interval that survives in the coefficient integral. Keep the $1/T$ factor and factor out the constant amplitude $A$.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Rectangular Periodic Signal
sections.section_title: Evaluating the Exponential Integral for Nonzero Harmonics

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=A$ on $0\le t<\tau$ and $0$ otherwise over period $T$, which expression equals $c_2$ after evaluating the restricted exponential integral?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set $k=2$ in the restricted-support formula. The nonzero-harmonic coefficient is $c_2=\frac{A}{T}\int_0^\tau e^{-j2\omega_0 t}\,dt$, and evaluating the exponential antiderivative gives $\frac{A}{T}\frac{1-e^{-j2\omega_0\tau}}{j2\omega_0}$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=2A$ on $0\le t<\tau$ and $0$ otherwise over period $T$, which expression equals $c_3$ after evaluating the restricted exponential integral?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set $k=3$ and keep the amplitude factor outside the integral. Then $c_3=\frac{2A}{T}\int_0^\tau e^{-j3\omega_0 t}\,dt$, so the antiderivative and endpoint evaluation give $\frac{2A}{T}\frac{1-e^{-j3\omega_0\tau}}{j3\omega_0}$.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Rectangular Periodic Signal
sections.section_title: Writing Rectangular-Signal Coefficients Using Amplitude, Width, Period, and Harmonic Index

prompt_blocks.text: Which piecewise expression correctly gives the complex Fourier coefficients $c_k$ for the rectangular periodic signal that equals $A$ on $0 \le t < \tau$ and $0$ otherwise over period $T$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The DC term is the average value, so $c_0=\frac{A\tau}{T}$. For $k\ne 0$, only the pulse-support interval contributes, and integrating $e^{-jk\omega_0 t}$ over $0 \le t < \tau$ gives $\frac{A}{-jk\omega_0 T}\left(e^{-jk\omega_0\tau}-1\right)$.

prompt_blocks.text: After substituting $\omega_0=\frac{2\pi}{T}$, which piecewise expression is equivalent for the same rectangular periodic signal?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: This is the same coefficient formula with $\omega_0=\frac{2\pi}{T}$ substituted. The DC term stays $\frac{A\tau}{T}$, and the nonzero-harmonic term becomes $\frac{A}{-j2\pi k}\left(e^{-j2\pi k\tau/T}-1\right)$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the DC Fourier-series coefficient for a rectangular periodic signal by converting duty cycle and signal levels into the average value over one period.

sections.section_title: Computing DC Value from a Given Duty Cycle

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic rectangular signal is $8$ for $\frac{1}{4}$ of each period and $0$ for the rest. What is its DC value?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the duty cycle $D=\frac{1}{4}$. The DC value is the high level times the duty cycle.
So the correct choice is $2$.

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic rectangular signal is $15$ for $0.4$ of each period and $0$ for the rest. What is its DC value?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the duty cycle $D=0.4$. The DC value is the high level times the duty cycle.
So the correct choice is $6$.

sections.section_title: Finding Duty Cycle from Pulse Width and Period

prompt_blocks.text: A rectangular signal is high for $2$ ms of every $7$ ms period and is $0$ otherwise. If the high level is $14$, what is its DC value?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Convert the pulse width and period into duty cycle first: $D = 2/7$. Then use the average-value formula with low level $0$: $14*(2/7)=4$.
So the DC value is $4$.

prompt_blocks.text: A rectangular signal is high for $5$ ms of every $12$ ms period and is $0$ otherwise. If the high level is $15$, what is its DC value?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Convert the pulse width and period into duty cycle first: $D = 5/12$. Then weight the high level by that fraction: $15*(5/12)=25/4$.
So the DC value is $25/4$.

sections.section_title: Computing DC Value for a Two-Level Rectangular Signal

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic rectangular signal is $8$ for $\frac{3}{5}$ of each period and $-2$ for the rest. What is its DC value?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the weighted average: the signal is $8$ for $\frac{3}{5}$ of the period, so $-2$ fills the remaining $\frac{2}{5}$.
That gives $\bar{x} = \frac{24}{5} - \frac{4}{5} = 4$, so the DC value is $4$.

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic rectangular signal is $5$ for $\frac{2}{5}$ of each period and $-2$ for the rest. What is its DC value?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the same weighted-average rule. The high level $5$ occupies $\frac{2}{5}$ of the period, and the low level $-2$ occupies $\frac{3}{5}$.
That simplifies to $\bar{x} = 2 - \frac{6}{5} = \frac{4}{5}$, so the DC value is $\frac{4}{5}$.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Zero DC Value from Balanced Signal Levels

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic rectangular signal is $8$ for $\frac{1}{3}$ of each period and $-4$ for the rest. What is its DC value?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the weighted average of the two levels over one period.
The positive and negative contributions cancel exactly, so the DC value is $0$.

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic rectangular signal is $6$ for $\frac{1}{4}$ of each period and $-2$ for the rest. What is its DC value?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Check the signed weighted contributions over one period.
The contributions are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign, so the DC value is $0$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Identify coefficient cancellations in the Fourier series coefficient formula to determine which even and odd harmonic indices of a periodic signal contribute nonzero spectral components.

sections.section_title: Identifying Even and Odd Harmonic Indices

prompt_blocks.text: Given the indices $k = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7$, choose the even harmonic indices and keep $k = 0$ separate as the DC term.

questions.correct_answer: The even harmonic indices are $\{2, 4, 6\}$, with $k = 0$ kept separate as the DC term.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The even indices in the list are $2$, $4$, and $6$. The DC term is $k = 0$, so it is not part of the even harmonic set.

prompt_blocks.text: Given the indices $k = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8$, choose the even harmonic indices and keep $k = 0$ separate as the DC term.

questions.correct_answer: The even harmonic indices are $\{2, 4, 6, 8\}$, with $k = 0$ kept separate as the DC term.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The even indices in the list are $2$, $4$, $6$, and $8$. The DC term is $k = 0$, so it stays separate from the even harmonic set.

sections.section_title: Detecting Even-Harmonic Cancellations

prompt_blocks.text: Given $c_k = 3B(1 + (-1)^k)$ for positive $k$, which harmonic indices are nonzero?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Test the parity factor. For even indices, $k = 2m$, so $(-1)^k = 1$ and $1 + (-1)^k = 2$. For odd indices, $k = 2m + 1$, so $(-1)^k = -1$ and $1 + (-1)^k = 0$.
So the even harmonics survive and the odd harmonics cancel.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $c_k = 5A(1 - (-1)^k)$ for positive $k$, which harmonic indices are nonzero?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Test the parity factor again. For even indices, $k = 2m$, so $(-1)^k = 1$ and $1 - (-1)^k = 0$. For odd indices, $k = 2m + 1$, so $(-1)^k = -1$ and $1 - (-1)^k = 2$.
So the odd harmonics survive and the even harmonics cancel. The prefactor $5A$ does not change which parity class survives.

sections.section_title: Detecting Odd-Harmonic Cancellations

prompt_blocks.text: Given $c_k = 4(1 + (-1)^k)$ for positive $k$, which harmonic indices are nonzero?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The prefactor $4$ does not change the parity test. Check the factor $1 + (-1)^k$ on even and odd indices.
So the odd harmonic coefficients vanish and the even harmonic coefficients remain nonzero.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $c_k = 3(1 + (-1)^k)$ for positive $k$, which harmonic indices are zero?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Again, the scalar $3$ only rescales the coefficients. The parity factor still determines which indices vanish.
So the odd harmonic coefficients are zero, and the even harmonic coefficients survive.

sections.section_title: Listing Nonzero Harmonics from a Coefficient Formula

prompt_blocks.text: Given $c_k = 3A(1 - (-1)^k) + 2B(1 + (-1)^k)$ for positive $k$, which harmonic families are nonzero?

choice_blocks.text: Both even and odd harmonics survive.

questions.correct_answer: Both even and odd harmonics survive.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Test the parity factor on even and odd positive indices.
Since both $c_{2m}$ and $c_{2m+1}$ are nonzero, both even and odd harmonic families survive.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $c_k = 5B(1 + (-1)^k) + 4A(1 - (-1)^k)$ for positive $k$, which harmonic families are nonzero?

choice_blocks.text: Both even and odd harmonics survive.

questions.correct_answer: Both even and odd harmonics survive.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Check the even and odd indices separately. The parity factors are still present, so neither harmonic family cancels completely.
Because both $c_{2m}$ and $c_{2m+1}$ are nonzero, both even and odd harmonic families survive.

entries.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Periodic Exponential
entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the complex Fourier-series coefficient integral for one period of an exponentially shaped periodic signal by combining the signal exponent with the harmonic kernel to obtain each harmonic coefficient.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Periodic Exponential
sections.section_title: Setting Up the One-Period Coefficient Integral

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{j3\omega_0 t}$ over one period $0 \le t < T$, which integral correctly sets up $c_2$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the complex Fourier-series coefficient formula over one full period. Keep the $\frac{1}{T}$ factor, the limits $0 \le t < T$, and the harmonic kernel $e^{-j2\omega_0 t}$.
That is the correct setup; do not simplify the exponent yet.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{j4\omega_0 t}$ over one period $0 \le t < T$, which integral correctly sets up $c_3$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The setup changes only the signal harmonic and the target coefficient index. The integral still uses one full period, the $\frac{1}{T}$ normalization, and the kernel $e^{-j3\omega_0 t}$.
This matches the example structure without changing the underlying step.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Periodic Exponential
sections.section_title: Combining Exponents in the Integrand

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{j5\omega_0 t}$, which simplified integrand appears inside $c_1$ after combining exponents?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Add the exponents in the product. Here $m=5$ and $k=1$, so the exponent becomes $j(m-k)\omega_0 t=j(5-1)\omega_0 t$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{j2\omega_0 t}$, which simplified integrand appears inside $c_5$ after combining exponents?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Combine the exponents and keep the complex oscillatory factor. Here $m=2$ and $k=5$, so the exponent becomes $j(m-k)\omega_0 t=j(2-5)\omega_0 t=-j3\omega_0 t$.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Periodic Exponential
sections.section_title: Evaluating Coefficients When the Combined Exponent Is Nonzero

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{j5\omega_0 t}$, what is $c_3$ after evaluating the nonzero combined exponent over one period?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The combined exponent is $e^{j(5-3)\omega_0 t}=e^{j2\omega_0 t}$. Because this is a nonmatching harmonic, its value over one full period cancels out.
So the coefficient is $0$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{j2\omega_0 t}$, what is $c_5$ after applying the same full-period cancellation?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Here the combined exponent is $e^{j(2-5)\omega_0 t}=e^{-j3\omega_0 t}$. It is still a nonmatching harmonic, so the one-period integral cancels out.
So the coefficient is again $0$.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Periodic Exponential
sections.section_title: Evaluating the Coefficient When the Combined Exponent Is Zero

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{j5\omega_0 t}$, what is $c_5$ when the combined exponent is zero?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set $k=5$ so the combined exponent is zero. The integrand becomes the constant $1$, so the coefficient is the normalized one-period integral of $1$.
The integral gives $T$, and the factor $1/T$ cancels it, so $c_5=1$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{j2\omega_0 t}$, what is $c_2$ when the combined exponent is zero?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set $k=2$ so the combined exponent is zero. That makes the integrand $1$, and the coefficient is the normalized integral over one period.
The period length cancels with the normalization, so the matching harmonic coefficient is $1$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute complex-valued Fourier series coefficients by evaluating the one-period complex-exponential coefficient integral and interpreting each result as the harmonic's amplitude-and-phase weight.

sections.section_title: Evaluating One Complex Coefficient Integral

prompt_blocks.text: What is $c_1$ for $x(t)=6\cos(\omega_0 t+\pi/6)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Expand the cosine as half the sum of complex exponentials, so the amplitude becomes $3$ instead of $6$. After multiplying by $e^{-j\omega_0 t}$, the matching $k=1$ term stays constant and the nonmatching term averages to zero over one period.
So $c_1=3e^{j\pi/6}$. The choice with the full amplitude misses the $1/2$ from the cosine expansion, the opposite-phase choice is the $k=-1$ coefficient, and the pure number ignores the phase weight.

prompt_blocks.text: What is $c_1$ for $x(t)=-8\cos(\omega_0 t-\pi/4)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The negative amplitude stays outside the cosine, and the cosine still contributes a half-amplitude coefficient. After you expand and multiply by $e^{-j\omega_0 t}$, only the matching harmonic remains.

So $c_1=-4e^{-j\pi/4}$. The choice with the full amplitude misses the $1/2$, the opposite-phase choice is the conjugate harmonic, the full-amplitude opposite-phase choice combines both mistakes, and the positive answer drops the sign on the original cosine.

sections.section_title: Simplifying a Coefficient into Rectangular Form

prompt_blocks.text: Simplify $c_1=3e^{j\pi/6}$ into rectangular form.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use Euler's formula, $e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta$, and keep the magnitude $3$ outside.
That simplifies to $\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}+\frac{3j}{2}$, so the correct choice is A.

prompt_blocks.text: Simplify $c_1=4e^{-j\pi/3}$ into rectangular form.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use Euler's formula and substitute the trigonometric values for $-\pi/3$.
So $c_1=2-2j\sqrt{3}$, which is choice A.

sections.section_title: Converting a Complex Coefficient to Magnitude and Phase

prompt_blocks.text: What are $|c_1|$ and $\angle c_1$ for $c_1=\sqrt{3}+j$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Take the magnitude from the right triangle formed by the real and imaginary parts.
The point $\sqrt{3}+j$ lies in quadrant I, so the phase is the first-quadrant reference angle $\pi/6$.
So the magnitude-and-phase pair is $2$ and $\pi/6$.

prompt_blocks.text: What are $|c_1|$ and $\angle c_1$ for $c_1=-\sqrt{3}+j$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the real and imaginary parts to get the magnitude.
Because the coefficient is in quadrant II, the phase is $2\pi/3$.
So the magnitude-and-phase pair is $2$ and $2\pi/3$.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Positive and Negative Harmonic Weights

prompt_blocks.text: For a real periodic signal with $c_4=2-j$ and $c_{-4}=2+j$, which statement best explains what these harmonic weights mean in the reconstruction?

choice_blocks.text: They are two unrelated amplitudes, one for the positive harmonic and one for the negative harmonic.
Only $c_4$ matters, because the negative-index coefficient can be ignored for real signals.
They are conjugate partners that together encode one real $k=4$ harmonic; the positive coefficient carries the amplitude-and-phase weight.
They are the instantaneous value of the signal at $t=4$.
They show that the signal must contain two separate $k=4$ oscillations.

questions.correct_answer: They are conjugate partners that together encode one real $k=4$ harmonic; the positive coefficient carries the amplitude-and-phase weight.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because the signal is real, $c_4$ and $c_{-4}$ must be conjugates. They do not represent two different harmonics; together they form one real oscillation, and the positive-index coefficient is the one whose magnitude and phase tell you the harmonic weight.

prompt_blocks.text: For a real periodic signal with $c_1=-3+4j$ and $c_{-1}=-3-4j$, which interpretation is correct?

choice_blocks.text: They are two unrelated amplitudes for different waves.
They are conjugate partners that together encode one real $k=1$ harmonic, with the positive coefficient carrying the amplitude-and-phase weight.
The negative coefficient is the only one that matters, so the positive coefficient can be dropped.
They are the value of the signal at $t=1$.
They mean the signal is complex-valued.

questions.correct_answer: They are conjugate partners that together encode one real $k=1$ harmonic, with the positive coefficient carrying the amplitude-and-phase weight.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A real signal requires conjugate symmetry, so $c_1$ and $c_{-1}$ are paired weights for one real harmonic. The positive coefficient carries the amplitude-and-phase information; the negative coefficient is its conjugate partner that makes the synthesis real.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert computed complex Fourier series coefficients into a magnitude spectrum by calculating |c_k| at DC and each positive and negative harmonic and interpreting the stem plot as the periodic signal's harmonic strength distribution.

sections.section_title: Computing Magnitudes of Complex Fourier Coefficients

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the magnitude formula $|a+bj|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$. Each coefficient is a conjugate of the other, so both magnitudes come out the same.
So the magnitude-spectrum stem heights at $k=2$ and $k=-2$ are both $25$.
A real coefficient still uses absolute value, so the sign disappears before you place the stem height on the spectrum.
So the two harmonic stems both have height $9$.

sections.section_title: Including the DC Coefficient in a Magnitude Spectrum

prompt_blocks.text: Given $c_0=-4$, $c_1=3-4j$, and $c_{-1}=3+4j$, what ordered set lists the magnitude-spectrum values at $k=0$, $k=1$, and $k=-1$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Include the DC term by the same absolute-value rule as the harmonic coefficients. The sign on $c_0$ does not survive on the magnitude spectrum.
So the ordered magnitude-spectrum values are $(4, 5, 5)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $c_0=8$, $c_1=1-j$, and $c_{-1}=1+j$, what magnitudes appear at $k=0$ and $k=\pm1$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The DC coefficient uses the same magnitude rule as the harmonic coefficients, so you take absolute value at $k=0$ too.
So the DC stem is $8$, and the two harmonic stems are both $\sqrt{2}$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute and interpret the phase spectrum by extracting the argument of each nonzero complex Fourier series coefficient and aligning those phases with the corresponding positive and negative harmonics of a periodic continuous-time signal.

sections.section_title: Extracting Phase from a Nonzero Complex Coefficient

prompt_blocks.text: Given $C_4 = -2 + 2\sqrt{3}j$, what is the principal phase at harmonic $k=4$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The real part is negative and the imaginary part is positive, so $C_4$ lies in quadrant II. The reference angle is $\pi/3$, which gives the principal phase $2\pi/3$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $C_{-3} = \sqrt{3} - j$, what is the principal phase at harmonic $k=-3$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The real part is positive and the imaginary part is negative, so $C_{-3}$ lies in quadrant IV. The reference angle is $\pi/6$, so the principal phase is $-\pi/6$.

sections.section_title: Assigning Phases to Positive and Negative Harmonics

prompt_blocks.text: Given $C_0 = -2$, $C_1 = 5e^{-j\pi/6}$, $C_{-1} = 5e^{j\pi/6}$, $C_2 = 0$, and $C_{-2} = 0$, which phase assignment across the harmonics $k=-2,-1,0,1,2$ is correct?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The DC coefficient is negative real, so its phase is $\pi$. The $k=\pm1$ pair keeps opposite signs, with $\phi_{-1}=\pi/6$ and $\phi_1=-\pi/6$. The zero coefficients at $k=\pm2$ stay blank.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $C_0 = 3$, $C_1 = 2e^{j\pi/2}$, $C_{-1} = 2e^{-j\pi/2}$, $C_2 = 1-j$, $C_{-2} = 1+j$, $C_3 = 0$, and $C_{-3} = 0$, which phase assignment across the harmonics $k=-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3$ is correct?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: $1-j$ has phase $-\pi/4$ and $1+j$ has phase $\pi/4$, so the $k=\pm2$ pair gets opposite signs. The $k=\pm1$ pair has phases $\pm\pi/2$, the DC term $3$ has phase $0$, and the zero coefficients at $k=\pm3$ stay blank.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Only nonzero coefficients get phase entries. Here $C_0$, $C_2$, and $C_{-2}$ are nonzero, so the phase spectrum keeps $k=0$ and $k=\pm2$. The zero coefficients at $k=\pm1$ are omitted entirely.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Only nonzero coefficients get phase entries. Here the nonzero coefficients are at $k=\pm1$ and $k=\pm3$, so those are the only harmonics that appear. The zero coefficients at $k=0$ and $k=\pm2$ are omitted entirely.

sections.section_title: Interpreting a Phase Spectrum from Fourier Coefficients

prompt_blocks.text: Given $C_0 = -2$, $C_1 = 4e^{j\pi/3}$, $C_{-1} = 4e^{-j\pi/3}$, $C_2 = 0$, $C_{-2} = 0$, $C_3 = 3e^{-j\pi/4}$, and $C_{-3} = 3e^{j\pi/4}$, which phase assignment across the harmonics $k=-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3$ is correct?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The negative DC term contributes phase $\pi$. The $k=\pm1$ and $k=\pm3$ coefficients are nonzero conjugate pairs, so their phases are opposite on $\pm k$. The $k=\pm2$ coefficients are zero, so they stay blank.
So the correct phase spectrum keeps the nonzero harmonics, gives the negative real DC term phase $\pi$, and leaves the zero harmonics out entirely.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $C_0 = 4$, $C_1 = 2e^{j\pi/6}$, $C_{-1} = 2e^{-j\pi/6}$, $C_2 = 5e^{-j\pi/2}$, $C_{-2} = 5e^{j\pi/2}$, $C_3 = 0$, and $C_{-3} = 0$, which phase assignment across the harmonics $k=-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3$ is correct?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The DC term is positive real, so its phase is $0$. The $k=\pm1$ pair gives phases $\pm\pi/6$, the $k=\pm2$ pair gives $\mp\pi/2$, and the zero coefficients at $k=\pm3$ stay blank.
So the correct phase spectrum keeps the two nonzero conjugate pairs, gives the positive DC term phase $0$, and omits the zero pair entirely.
